facts.title: Found by a Blue Line
facts.text: Indium was discovered in 1863 by German chemists Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymus Theodor Richter at the Freiberg Mining Academy while searching for thallium in zinc ores. When they heated a sample and examined its light through a spectroscope, they saw an unexpected brilliant indigo-blue spectral line that matched no known element. They named the new metal 'indium' after that indigo color, from the Latin 'indicum'.

facts.title: It Screams When You Bend It
facts.text: Indium is so soft you can cut it with a knife and even dent it with a fingernail. When you bend a bar of pure indium, it emits a faint crackling sound known as a 'tin cry,' caused by the rearrangement of crystal planes inside the metal. This same effect is famously heard in tin, indium's neighbor in the periodic table.

facts.title: Stays Liquid in the Cold
facts.text: Indium melts at a low 156.6 degrees Celsius, but its real superpower is staying solid and ductile at extreme cold. Unlike most metals, it does not become brittle at cryogenic temperatures, so it is used as a sealing gasket and thermal contact material in equipment cooled to near absolute zero. Pressing two clean indium surfaces together can even form a vacuum-tight 'cold weld' seal.

facts.title: The Glass That Conducts
facts.text: A compound called indium tin oxide (ITO) is both transparent and electrically conductive, a rare combination that makes it indispensable to modern screens. Almost every smartphone, tablet, and LCD television uses an invisible ITO coating as the touch-sensitive, current-carrying layer on the glass. This single application consumes the majority of the world's indium production each year.

facts.title: A Byproduct, Never the Goal
facts.text: There are essentially no indium mines, because the element is too rare and dispersed to be worth extracting on its own. Instead, nearly all indium is recovered as a byproduct when zinc sulfide ores are refined, where it hides in the mineral sphalerite. China, South Korea, Japan, and Canada lead its production, recovering it from the residues left after zinc smelting.

facts.title: Rarer Than Silver
facts.text: Indium makes up only about 0.05 parts per million of Earth's crust, making it roughly three times scarcer than silver. Because supplies are limited and demand from electronics is high, indium is classified as a critical raw material by both the European Union and the United States. Recycling old screens and sputtering targets has become an important secondary source.

facts.title: Mirrors for Astronomers
facts.text: Because indium clings tightly to glass and resists tarnishing, it can be deposited as a thin, highly reflective film. In the mid-20th century, before aluminum coatings dominated, indium was used to make mirrors for telescopes and other precision optical instruments. Its excellent reflectivity across visible and infrared light made it valuable for specialized scientific optics.

facts.title: Forged in Dying Stars
facts.text: Indium is not made in ordinary stellar burning; it is created in violent cosmic events through neutron-capture processes. The slow process (the s-process) inside aging giant stars and the rapid process (the r-process) in neutron-star collisions both build up heavy elements like indium. Its cosmic rarity on Earth directly reflects how inefficiently these dramatic processes produce it.

facts.title: An Almost-Eternal Isotope
facts.text: Natural indium is mostly indium-115, which is technically radioactive but astonishingly stable. Its half-life is about 4.4 times ten to the fourteenth years, more than 30,000 times longer than the current age of the universe. This decay is so slow that indium-115 is effectively stable, and you would never notice the rare beta particles it gives off.

facts.title: Toxic, With No Job in Life
facts.text: Indium has no known biological role; no living organism uses it for any function. In its place, indium compounds can be harmful, and inhaling fine indium tin oxide dust has caused a serious lung disease called indium lung in some factory workers. On the medical side, however, the radioactive tracer indium-111 is deliberately attached to white blood cells and injected to help doctors locate hidden infections and tumors in nuclear-medicine scans.
